query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the CoCrFeNi matrix with a small fraction of tungsten (W), on the order of 0.5 at.%, will induce formation of stable lubricious oxide phases that maintain a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix (produced by conventional melting or powder metallurgy) exhibiting elevated friction and wear above ~500 °C due to oxide film breakdown and substrate softening.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.5 at.% tungsten into the CoCrFeNi matrix during alloy synthesis (e.g., vacuum arc melting).
generation.conditions: Continuous sliding contact from room temperature to 800 °C under moderate normal loads (e.g., 5–10 N) in air or inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: A tungsten-enriched oxide tribofilm that develops during sliding and regulates friction and wear across the entire temperature range.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten promotes the formation of stable oxide islands within the tribofilm, preserving low shear strength and preventing extensive abrasive or adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi baseline, friction decreases by ~15–25% and wear volume is reduced by up to an order of magnitude in the 25–800 °C range.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi tends to exhibit friction coefficients exceeding ~0.4 under higher temperatures and normal loads, with more rapid oxide film breakdown and softening-induced wear.
generation.boundary: This improvement persists up to ~800 °C at moderate loads; behavior beyond these ranges remains unverified and requires further testing.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal tungsten content is not fully determined; extreme loads, higher doping levels, or long-term stability in non-air environments remain underexplored.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture both the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and a CoCrFeNi–0.5 at.% W alloy under identical processing conditions. Perform pin-on-disk tribology tests at incremental temperatures (25, 200, 400, 600, 800 °C) in air under constant load to measure friction and wear.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at each temperature
Wear volume via profilometry or mass loss
Surface and cross-sectional SEM/EDS to identify oxide tribofilm formation
XRD of wear tracks to confirm tungsten-containing oxides
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W-doped alloy does not yield demonstrably lower friction (~15–25% reduction) or significantly reduced wear compared to undoped CoCrFeNi across all test temperatures, the hypothesis is invalid.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. High Temperature Friction and Wear Properties of HEA Coatings
cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 shows the influence of the W powder addition on the high temperature friction and wear properties of the AlCoCrFeNiWx coatings on H13 steel. The H13 steel exhibits a maximum friction coefficient and wear loss after 800 °C/60 min high temperature friction and wear treatment. Compared to the H13 steel, all HEA coatings exhibit smaller friction coefficient and wear loss. A minimum friction coefficient and wear loss (only 12% of H13 steel wear loss) occurs in the AlCoCrFeNiWx with the addition of 0.5 at.% W. Consequently, a great improvement in the high temperature friction and wear resistance is achieved by the addition of the W powder and is likely due to the lattice distortion becoming more remarkable; the unmelted W-rich particles also improve the wear resistance as the hard phase. The addition of 0.5 at.% W powder in AlCoCrFeNi HEA system can improve its high temperature friction and wear resistance. These results are also supported by wear scars height and width of samples. The distinct differences are observed with regard to three-dimensional morphologies, as shown in Figure 7.
